source: original; stimulus is a data table from the U.S. Census Bureau, table HS-42

stimulus.source_note: Data table from U.S. Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract of the United States, table HS-42 (Selected Communications Media, 1920 to 2001).
stimulus.text:
| Year | Share of American households owning a television |
| 1950 | 9.0% |
| 1955 | 64.5% |
| 1960 | 87.1% |

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract, table HS-42. The table gives the share of households owning at least one television set.

stem: The table best supports which conclusion about television by 1960?

options.text: Television had replaced radio as the main source of news
options.misconception: The table counts television sets only, and it says nothing about radio or news.

options.text: Most American homes still had no television set
options.misconception: The table shows the opposite: 87 of 100 homes owned a set by 1960.

options.text: Television had become a fixture in most American homes
Television ownership grew slowly through the 1950s
options.misconception: The table shows fast growth, from 9 in 100 homes to 87 in 100 in ten years.

rationales.A: The table says nothing about radio or about news, so it cannot show that television replaced radio.
rationales.B: The table shows 87.1 percent of homes owned a set in 1960, so most homes had one.
rationales.C: By 1960, 87 of 100 homes owned a television, so the set had become a normal part of the home.
rationales.D: The table shows a jump from 9 percent to 87 percent in one decade, which is fast growth, not slow.
rationales.general:
1. Read the table across the rows: 9 homes in 100 had a set in 1950, and 87 in 100 had one by 1960.
2. That is a jump from a rare luxury to something nearly every home owned.
3. A device that common shapes what a whole country watches and talks about.
Remember: When a table shows a steep rise to near-universal use, the safe conclusion is that the thing became ordinary, not rare.
